parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman enrols on an evening language course.
script: Good evening, City Adult Education, Dan speaking.
Hi. I'd like to enrol on one of your evening language courses.
Great. Can I have your name?
Priyanka Bose. B, O, S, E.
Thank you. Which language are you interested in?
Spanish. I'm going travelling in South America next year.
A little, at school, but that was years ago. I can only remember a few words.
Then I'd suggest the elementary course rather than complete beginners. It reviews the basics quickly.
The elementary class runs on Monday evenings from six thirty to eight thirty, in room fourteen.
The course fee is a hundred and eighty pounds for twelve weeks. Do you live in the city?
Then you're entitled to a ten percent discount for local residents.
Oh, great. Is the textbook included?
No, it's extra. It costs twenty-five pounds, and you can buy it on the first evening.
Her name's Lucia. She's from Mexico, so you'll hear Latin American Spanish, which will be useful for your trip.
And at the end of the course, the class usually goes to a Spanish restaurant, where everyone has to order in Spanish.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: An organiser describes a community repair café.
script: Hello everyone, and welcome. I'm Joan, and I started the Northside Repair Café three years ago.

The idea came from seeing how much was being thrown away in our area, from toasters to trousers, often because of very small faults. Our aim is to reduce waste by helping people repair things instead of replacing them.
We're open on the first Saturday of every month, from ten until two, in the church hall.
There's no charge for repairs. We do have a donations box for anyone who'd like to contribute towards costs like spare parts.
The most common items people bring are lamps, followed by clothes and bicycles.
Let me explain where to go when you arrive. At table one, Mike and his team fix electrical items such as lamps, kettles and radios. Please don't bring anything that's still under warranty.
At table two, Asha and her helpers repair clothes. They can replace zips, fix holes and shorten trousers.
Bicycles are repaired outside, in the yard, because they take up so much space.
At table three, Tom deals with furniture: wobbly chairs, broken drawers and so on.
Table four is for computers and phones. They can help with things like replacing batteries.
And in the children's corner, there's a volunteer who repairs toys, which is always very popular.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two media students, Kai and Laila, discuss their documentary about a fishing village.
script: Laila, let's talk about our documentary on the fishing village before we start editing.
OK. I think we've agreed that the main focus should be how the fishermen are coping with the decline in fish stocks.
Yes. That's the strongest story. The problem is, on our first filming trip, the wind was so strong that it ruined most of the sound.
I know. We should borrow a better microphone from the department, one with a wind cover.
Good idea. And how long should the film be? The limit is twenty minutes.
I think twelve minutes is about right. Any longer and it might drag.
Agreed. Dr Kaur said we should let the fishermen tell the story in their own words, and use as little narration as possible.
That makes sense. Let's go through the scenes. The sunrise shots of the boats leaving the harbour are beautiful.
I think we should move them to the very beginning, as the opening.
Yes. The interview with the fish seller at the market works well. Keep that.
The harbour master's interview is important, but the sound is terrible. We'll have to film it again.
And the drone footage? We didn't actually get permission to fly over the harbour, so I don't think we can use it.
You're right. We'll cut it. What about the night fishing scene?
That's the best thing we've filmed. Definitely keep it.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on how bats use echolocation.
script: Today we're going to talk about bats, and in particular about the remarkable way many of them find their way in the dark.
There are more than one thousand four hundred species of bat, which means they make up about a fifth of all mammal species. They are the only mammals capable of true flight.
Many bats hunt using echolocation. They produce calls and listen for the echoes that bounce back from objects around them. Most of these calls are ultrasonic, too high-pitched for humans to hear.
Echolocation was discovered in 1938 by the American scientist Donald Griffin, who used a special detector that could pick up ultrasonic sounds.
The precision is extraordinary. Some bats can detect objects as thin as a human hair in complete darkness.
As a bat approaches an insect, it calls faster and faster, producing what scientists call a feeding buzz, so that it can track the insect's exact position in the final moments before catching it.
Some insects have developed defences. Certain moths can hear bat calls and dive to escape, and some even produce their own clicks, which seem to confuse the bat's echolocation.

Bats are extremely valuable to humans. They eat huge numbers of insects, including crop pests, and some species are important for pollination. The plant used to make tequila, for example, is pollinated by bats.

Unfortunately, many bat populations are declining. Large numbers are killed by wind turbines, and in North America, a disease called white-nose syndrome, caused by a fungus, has killed millions of bats during hibernation.

passages.title: Guiding Lights
paragraphs: For more than two thousand years, lighthouses have guided sailors away from dangerous rocks and towards safe harbours. The most famous early example was the Pharos of Alexandria in Egypt, built in the third century BC. Estimated to have been over 100 metres tall, it was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. A fire burned at its top, and some accounts claim that mirrors were used to reflect its light far out to sea. Damaged by a series of earthquakes, it had collapsed completely by the fifteenth century.

For centuries, lighthouses relied on simple fires, and later on candles and oil lamps, and many were poorly built. The story of the Eddystone Lighthouse, on a group of rocks off the coast of Plymouth in England, shows how difficult construction could be. The first lighthouse there, a wooden tower designed by Henry Winstanley, was completed in 1698. In 1703, a violent storm swept it away, killing Winstanley, who was inside carrying out repairs. Altogether, the Eddystone lighthouse has been rebuilt four times.

The third Eddystone lighthouse, completed in 1759 by the engineer John Smeaton, was a turning point. Smeaton built it of granite blocks that were cut to lock into each other, so that the whole structure acted as a single mass. He also used a type of lime that set underwater. His tower stood for over a century and became the model for lighthouses around the world. It was eventually replaced, not because it failed, but because the rock beneath it was being worn away.

The light itself was transformed in 1822, when the French physicist Augustin Fresnel invented a new kind of lens. Instead of a single heavy piece of glass, it used rings of glass prisms to bend and concentrate the light into a powerful beam. Lighthouses fitted with Fresnel lenses could be seen from more than thirty kilometres away.

For most of their history, lighthouses were staffed by keepers, who lived at the lighthouse, often in isolated and dangerous conditions, and kept the lamp burning through the night. During the twentieth century, lighthouses were gradually automated. In Britain, the last keepers left in 1998.

Today, ships navigate mainly by satellite systems such as GPS, and some people question whether lighthouses are still needed. However, many remain in operation as a backup, since electronic systems can fail. Others have been preserved as historic monuments, and some have found new lives as museums or hotels.

passages.title: Printing a House
paragraphs: Most people associate 3D printing with small plastic objects. But in recent years, engineers have built printers large enough to produce entire buildings. These machines, which may sit on rails or move on robotic arms, push out a thick, fast-setting concrete mixture through a nozzle, building up walls layer by layer according to a digital design.

Supporters argue that the technology could make construction much faster and cheaper. In 2017, a company printed the walls of a small house in Russia in about 24 hours, on site, in winter conditions. Because the walls are printed by machine, fewer workers are needed, and labour is one of the largest costs in construction.

3D printing also gives architects new freedom. Curved walls, which are expensive and difficult to build with bricks or concrete blocks, are no harder to print than straight ones. And because the printer places material only where it is needed, the process can produce much less waste than traditional methods, in which materials are often cut to size and discarded.

Some of the most promising projects aim to provide homes for people in need. In 2019, a charity and a construction technology company began printing houses for a community of low-income families in the state of Tabasco in Mexico, families who had previously lived in unsafe shelters. The houses were designed with the residents and built to withstand earthquakes.

There are, however, significant obstacles. In many countries, building regulations were written for traditional methods and have not yet been adapted to printed structures, making approval slow and uncertain. Questions remain about the long-term strength of printed concrete. Moreover, printers can currently produce only the walls; roofs, windows, plumbing and electrical systems still have to be installed using conventional methods. Some critics also worry about the loss of skilled construction jobs.

Looking further ahead, 3D printing may allow construction in places where traditional methods are impossible. NASA has run a competition to design habitats that could be printed on the Moon or Mars, using materials found on the surface rather than transported from Earth. What sounds like science fiction may one day become a practical way to build beyond our planet.

passages.title: Are Video Games Good for You?
paragraphs: Video games have long been blamed for a range of social problems, from poor school results to violence. Yet over the past two decades, researchers have found that some kinds of gaming can have measurable benefits. As with most questions about technology, the answer depends on which games, how much, and for whom.

Some of the most interesting findings concern fast-paced action games. The cognitive scientist Daphne Bavelier and her colleagues found that people who regularly played such games performed better than non-players on several tests of visual attention, such as tracking several moving objects at once and spotting small details in a cluttered scene. Importantly, some studies showed that non-players who were trained on action games improved too, suggesting that the games caused the improvement rather than simply attracting people who were already skilled.

Specially designed games may also help older people. In a study published in 2013, researchers led by Adam Gazzaley created a driving game called NeuroRacer, in which players had to steer while responding to signs. Older adults who trained on the game improved their ability to multitask, and some of the improvements lasted for months. There is even evidence from medicine: studies of surgeons have found that those who play video games tend to make fewer errors in certain types of keyhole surgery, which require precise hand-eye coordination.

The debate about violence has been more heated. Laboratory studies often measure aggression in indirect ways, for example by allowing participants to give an opponent unpleasant loud noises or very spicy hot sauce. Some such studies have found small increases in aggression after violent games. However, in my view, there is no convincing evidence that violent games lead to serious real-world violence or criminal behaviour, and many researchers have criticised the way laboratory aggression is measured.

There are genuine risks, though. In 2019, the World Health Organization included 'gaming disorder' in its international classification of diseases. The condition is diagnosed only when gaming seriously harms a person's daily life, such as their education, work or relationships, for at least a year. Most researchers believe it affects only a small minority of players, but for those people the consequences can be severe.

Not all games are alike. Puzzle and strategy games may develop planning and problem-solving skills, while games designed to keep players spending money can encourage unhealthy habits. I believe that rather than banning or praising gaming as a whole, parents should pay attention to which games their children play and for how long.

task1.text: The table below shows the composition of household waste, by percentage, in one city in 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The table compares the proportions of different types of material in household waste in one city in 2000 and 2020.

Overall, the most significant changes were a sharp fall in the share of paper and a dramatic rise in the share of plastic. Food waste overtook paper to become the largest category, while the other materials changed only slightly.
In 2000, paper was the largest component of household waste, at 35%, followed by food at 30%. Plastic and glass each made up 10%, while metal accounted for 8% and other materials for 7%.

By 2020, the share of paper had fallen to just 20%, whereas plastic had more than doubled to 22%, making it the second largest category. Food waste rose to 35%, the highest proportion of any material. Meanwhile, the figures for glass and metal fell slightly, to 8% and 6% respectively, and the proportion of other materials increased marginally to 9%.

task2.text: Some people think that all secondary school students should be required to do unpaid community service, such as helping in hospitals or cleaning parks, as part of their education. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
model: In some countries, secondary school students must complete a certain number of hours of community service before they graduate. I agree that schools should require some unpaid community work, as long as the programme is well organised and students have some choice in what they do.

The main benefit of community service is that it teaches young people about responsibility and the needs of others. Students who spend time helping elderly people in care homes, tutoring younger children or cleaning up local parks are likely to develop empathy and a sense of connection to their community. These experiences are rarely provided by classroom lessons. Community service can also help students develop practical skills, such as communication, teamwork and time management, which will be useful in their future careers. Some students may even discover an interest that shapes their choice of university course or profession.

Critics argue that compulsory volunteering is a contradiction, since true volunteering should be freely chosen. They also point out that students already face heavy academic workloads, and that forcing them to do extra unpaid work may create resentment rather than a genuine desire to help. In addition, poorly organised schemes can leave students doing meaningless tasks that benefit no one.

These are valid concerns, but they can be addressed. The number of required hours should be moderate, perhaps one afternoon a month, and students should be allowed to choose from a range of activities that match their interests. Schools should also work with local organisations to make sure the work is genuinely useful.
In conclusion, I believe that a well-designed programme of community service would benefit both students and society, and should therefore be part of secondary education.

speaking.cue:
Describe something you made by hand.
You should say:
- what you made
- how you made it
- how long it took
and explain how you felt about it.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about a small wooden bookshelf I made last year. I'd been wanting more space for my books for ages, and instead of buying one, I decided to try making it myself, partly because I'm always looking for new challenges. I'd never done any woodwork before, so I watched quite a few online videos first. Then I bought some pine boards from a timber shop near my house and borrowed a saw and a drill from my uncle, who used to be a carpenter. He gave me a lot of advice, especially about measuring carefully, because my first attempt at cutting a shelf was about two centimetres too short. The whole thing took me about three weekends. After cutting and screwing the pieces together, I sanded the wood until it was smooth and painted it a dark green colour. It's definitely not perfect. If you look closely, one shelf is slightly crooked. But I'm really proud of it, because it was something I created from nothing, and every time I put a book on it, I remember how much I learned in the process. It also made me realise how satisfying it is to work with your hands after spending so many hours in front of a computer.
